lines: When the plan's account is saved in a terminal that is logged into another account, the calculator offers Log into beside Arm. One press logs that terminal into the plan's account through the terminal's own Login window, with the password the terminal saved, and without restarting it. The product never sees or types the password.

If the account the terminal shows has open positions or orders, the calculator asks once more before it switches, because that terminal will not show them until you log back. If the terminal has no saved password for the account, or its server asks for a one-time password, the Login window opens ready for you to finish.

Log into does not appear while the account the terminal shows carries a running hedge, or when the terminal runs the desk and the plan's account is on another broker's server, where the desk cannot start. The bar says why instead. If the account is already open in another terminal, the press says so and changes nothing.

Today tells you what to do on each running account. For an account short of its goal, it asks you to trade it your own way and shows the day's room and the most one position may risk. Once the goal is reached (a challenge's target, or Withdraw at on a real account), it asks only for the smallest position your broker allows, and only while trading days are still owed.

Under each account, Today shows what comes next: the odds of reaching the goal before the floor, and what to do either way, such as asking for the next stage if the challenge passes, or the plan to buy if it fails. When today's position can decide the plan, Today says so and measures, on the terminal's own history, how often a buy or a sell of your last position's size would have reached the goal first.

A real account that has not traded since it was funded has its room for the day again, on Today, on its plan and in the calculator. An account that has never traded counts its days without a trade from the day it arrived, so its last day to trade shows as well.
Today no longer asks you to buy accounts past the firm's limit on how many you may hold at once, and a room whose figures cannot be worked out shows as not known instead of $0.
The record on Today shows each plan once a day, and the days a passed challenge waits for its next account no longer count as days you left untouched.
Not today on an account close to the firm's limit of days without a trade puts the day away in one press.

The calculator's star on Buy or Sell is filled only when the gap between the two holds up across whole days of history. Otherwise it is open and dashed, which means that side only leans, and its sentence says how much chance alone could move the gap.
The calculator groups the digits of a very large ceiling, and the figure beside a target says what it sets aside for costs. A target you type in yourself sets nothing aside, so it shows no figure.

The application now opens on Today. It lists what only you can do today across every plan, how much of each account's room for the day is left, what the firm owes you and what falls due soon. It also shows how each recent day used its room, and how many trading days each plan has to its floor, at full use and at your pace.
Windows notifications now tell you when a plan burns or is ready for its next account, when money is waiting for you, when a deadline is near, and an hour before the day's room runs out.

A plan's card draws its path in boxes. The challenges stand in one row, each with its dates, result, trading days and money, and the funded accounts have a lane of their own below. The account being traded opens inside its own box with the firm's rules on it: what one position may risk, what is left today and to the floor, the trading days and the payout's date, each turning amber near its limit. A lane under the path marks the dates ahead.

Arm now keeps the firm's hard rules. Once you say you have asked for a payout, nothing opens on that plan until it arrives. A challenge past its target takes only the smallest volume while trading days are still owed. No order starts inside the firm's weekend, and a position on an instrument that trades through it, such as crypto, is closed before it begins. The calculator says which rule holds before you press, and both keep a small margin inside the firm's limits: 0.2% of the balance unless you change it under Sizing a hedge in Settings.

ProopCo plans follow the firm's own published rules: each family's drawdown and timing rules, trading days counted without weekends, payout dates and the split set by the payout option you bought, and the price refunded from the third payout. A Flex account's daily floor rises with the day's profit, as ProopCo measures it. Proop ONE can now be recorded, and reading a real account's payout no longer fails once it has traded.

On a real ProopCo Economy account, a position may risk 2% of the balance and Arm waits five minutes after one closes. The calculator warns when one symbol's run would bring more than 80% of the target. A plan's last challenge waits when its real account would take you over the firm's cap on real accounts, counting only the accounts of the person the plan belongs to.

The calculator's Buy and Sell now show how often each side reached your target before your stop, measured on the prop terminal's own history, on the one-minute timeframe unless you choose another in Settings. A star marks the side the figures favour for your goal, and the panel behind the i shows how past trades like yours ended and how much of any gap chance alone would give.
A note on a plan can be styled with bold, italic, a highlight and lists. Notes you wrote before read exactly as they did, and the pin in the calculator opens every pinned note in full.
The application has a dark theme. It follows Windows unless you choose light or dark in Settings, and every screen was checked for readability in it.

An eye in the header hides every amount of money and every account number, on every screen and in notifications, until you press it again. Prices, lots and percentages stay, and the Excel export and journals keep the real figures.
Screen readers now name every field on the Settings page.

The Overview opens on your own money: the cash you have actually made. Beside it, when there is any, are what a funded account holds for you after the split, what your open hedges are floating, and what is left after your running costs. Below it are your earnings over time and four links, to Plans, Hedges, Cash and Costs. Figures that added the prop account's result to your broker money are gone.

Everything about one plan has moved onto that plan's card, into a Details row that stays folded until you open it. Its tabs show what each account earned, how each challenge moved, the plan's own payments and how its hedges went.

Cash and Costs are new pages in the sidebar. Cash lists every fee, refund and payout, and your own trading at the brokers. Costs shows what trading cost you in commission, swap, fees and spread, and what you paid for accounts.

Win rate, profit factor and the other hedge statistics now count each hedge by its real result, the figure in the Real result column on the Hedges page. They used to add the prop side and the broker side together, so a challenge hedge that made you money at the broker could count as a loss because the prop account lost more. Expect these figures to change after the update. The Excel export counts them the same way on its dashboard and its By instrument sheet, and the Hedges page has a new card saying how the hedges went.

Plans can hold notes. On a plan's card, write as many as you like, either a note for the positions still to come or a lesson the plan taught you, and pin, edit or delete any of them later. They stay folded into one line with their count until you open them, and the plan's heading shows how many of each it has. Closing a plan offers a box for what it taught you, and a finished plan with no lesson offers to add one.
When the plan you are sizing has pinned notes, the calculator's top bar shows a pin with their number. Press it to read them, with a link to the plan's card.

The header is new. The page you are on, your journal and the clock are on the left, and one row of status chips is on the right, kept to one line on every screen. When something waits for your decision, an icon with the count appears there. Pressing it opens the decisions window again, even after you chose Later.

While a page loads, you see the product's mark with its two legs moving and a line saying what is coming, where grey placeholder bars used to be. It appears only when loading takes more than a moment, and it stays still if you have asked your computer for less motion.

The suggested hedge ratio now keeps a passing hedge inside your pass budget. If the hedge passes the challenge, the broker side never loses more than what is left of the stage's budget plus what it has already earned. The rail and the chart both mark that ratio, and when the suggestion is on it, one label says both.

The risk in the calculator now has a padlock, like the lots and the stop. The three depend on each other, so you can lock two of them at most. The calculator works out the third and says which two it came from.
You can give the hedge ratio as broker lots as well as a percentage. Type the broker lots and the ratio follows. Lock either one and it stays put, whatever else changes.

Beside the prop lots and the broker lots, the calculator shows the margin each position takes and what share of the account's balance that is. The reward to risk of the stop and the target is shown under their two boxes.
What it costs to get into a trade, the spread and the commission, now sits under the stop and target outcomes on the right.
The calculator's working indicator no longer flickers while you follow the market, or while your risk follows a limit that moves with the equity. It shows only after a change you made.
The calculator notices within seconds when a terminal is switched to another account. It used to take about two minutes.
Opening the calculator straight from its address no longer stops following the market with a message that the price could not be read.
The calculator's ratio chart no longer prints a stray 0 at the end of its zero line, and on a phone-width screen its legend no longer covers it.

When the broker account cannot carry the prop side winning, Arm now asks you instead of refusing. A window explains that the broker may close the leg early, and Arm anyway carries on. A new setting, When the broker account is short, chooses whether to ask, refuse or allow.

The window that asks before firing shows live prices for a plan that follows the market. For a plan at a set level, it warns when the price has passed a level or moved further than your tolerance, and Fire stays off while that is true. Wait here is now called Place pending orders and says what it does, and Enter at market gives up the level and follows the price instead.
When a server lists an instrument's name as close-only or disabled, Arm says so and shows where to choose the name that still trades, instead of telling you to wait for a session to open.

When an instrument has two names on a server, the name to trade is now chosen for the whole server instead of account by account. A new account uses the live name from its first read, judged from what the terminal says about each name and from the server's latest orders. What you set for single accounts becomes one setting for their server, and Settings, Catalogues lists each server once, with the instruments you trade first.

Setting up a broker terminal now puts the desk on a chart the terminal saves and turns Algo Trading on in the terminal's own settings. Closing the terminal, restarting Windows or switching its account no longer undoes either. The set-up asks for your agreement again, because its list of steps has grown.

After an update installs, the card at the foot of the sidebar shows the desk being put on your terminals one by one while you keep working. The window saying the update is done appears once that has finished, and names any terminal it left alone.

A terminal you close and start again is driven again within half a minute. Closing the desk's chart shows on the terminal's card within a second, and choosing a route or arming while a terminal is still connecting is answered in seconds instead of waiting for a retry.

A plan's card shows the hedge running on its account: a bracket under the progress bar from where the stop would leave the balance to where the target would, a live mark at the equity, and one line saying what is floating and what each level comes to.
On a hedge that is still open, each open leg pulses at its live end and shows what it is floating, updated every time the terminal is read.

The Hedge operations table draws its rows as you scroll instead of all at once, so the page opens faster however many hedges you have. Sorting any long table now sorts the whole list, not only the rows already drawn.

The totals under the Hedge operations table always add up every row the filters leave, including rows not drawn yet. The instrument and status filters in the table's own columns narrow the rows again; they had stopped doing anything.

Arriving at Hedge operations from a plan shows which account the table is narrowed to. The dropdown names it, and clearing it brings every hedge back. An empty table says why it is empty: the account or person chosen, the status, or a column filter.

Marking an unreconciled hedge as reviewed now settles it. It reads Closed with a reviewed badge and leaves the Unreconciled list, while its evidence still says the two sources disagree. Hedges you had already accepted are settled the same way after the update. A hedge that starts raising something new after you accepted it no longer shows as reviewed: it asks again, and you can accept it as it now stands.

The Excel export opens on a dashboard with the Overview's figures and five charts: the running result, the result by month, by plan and by instrument, and what trading cost. New sheets break the record down by day, by instrument and by kind of cost, the hedges and plans sheets have more columns, and every table has a header that stays in view, filters, and your own money in green and red. Every sheet and column the old file had is still where it was.
Printing the export spreads wide sheets such as Hedge operations across several pages at a size you can read, with the first column repeated on each page.
Every page opens at its top, and pressing a page in the sidebar changes it straight away. Opening Hedges used to take several seconds on a large record.

Explanations that should appear when you rest the pointer on a badge or a figure now do, for example on a hedge's Real result and on its "placed here" and "paired by hand" badges. Many of them never opened before.
On a phone-width screen, card titles no longer disappear and the Hedges page no longer scrolls sideways.

There is a new News page. It shows MetaTrader's economic calendar with MetaQuotes' forecasts, the actual figures and the day of the week. It warns you before a release that moves what you trade, opens a window before one that moves a position you have open, and tells you when the market moves with no news scheduled.

For each release, the News page says what a figure above or below the forecast usually does to gold, or to whichever instrument you follow. It takes this from written rules where there are any and from your terminal's own history where there are not, and says how often it has held on your terminal.
When a figure comes out, the release stays at the top of the News page for fifteen minutes, with how far the instrument has moved since.

The News page, and a new News card on the Overview, show today's market hours on a timeline from midnight to midnight. The Sydney, Tokyo, London and New York sessions each have their own row and colour, another row names the hours when they overlap, and the timeline also shows when each instrument you follow trades at your broker and when your releases are due.
When you move the mouse over the timeline, a line follows it with the exact time and a card says what is open at that minute.
High-importance releases are shown in red and moderate ones in orange. Every instrument, currency and trading region on the News page carries its logo or flag.

The application now checks this computer's clock against the internet. If the clock is more than thirty seconds out, it asks you to set it right, because the time of every trade is measured against it.
The Fire window now shows the warnings the Arm check raises, such as a market session about to close.
"Keep them open" in the market-closing window no longer reports a failure after it worked.

With the lots locked and the stop free, typing or dragging the risk now moves the stop to where those lots lose that much, never more. With both locked, the risk is shown as a readout that tells you which padlock to open. The stop and target boxes also keep every decimal the instrument quotes.

On a funded plan the calculator can now size and place a prop position with no broker leg. Its target sits at a reward to risk of 0.2 by default, and the risk starts at 98% of what the account may risk. The application records the position as your own trade rather than a hedge and, like a hedge, closes it before the market shuts.

The calculator now estimates commission for each instrument from what that instrument has actually been charged. It used to use one average across everything the account traded, which on bitcoin understated the cost about fourteen times.
The calculator answers faster, most of all on a record with many prop accounts. While it works out a new answer, the figures fade and a thin line runs along the top until the new ones arrive.

The figures on screen keep up with the terminals when some of the terminals you added are closed. The last-read time in the header, the floating result of an open hedge and the calculator's one-hedge-per-plan check all update as the terminals are read, and the running terminals are read at the interval you set.
The clock in the header now ticks every second instead of jumping every few seconds.
On a slower computer, pages no longer say "The local reporting service is unavailable" while the service is starting. They wait, keep what they already show, and fill in by themselves.
Before every update the application keeps a copy of your data, now also when the update is installed as the application starts. It keeps the three most recent copies instead of the oldest ones.

The magic number on each leg can now be left empty, and a new setup starts with it empty. It used to be impossible to clear, and it began at a number nobody had chosen. MetaTrader reads an empty one as no magic, and nothing in the application needs one.
The four trailing stop rules now fit on the page, each explained on its own line. The fourth used to run off the edge of the card.
The two instrument lists in Settings are now tables of a fixed height that scroll inside themselves, so the page no longer grows with every instrument your accounts offer.
The broker's stop-out line now leaves the chart when the last position closes. It used to stay behind, showing a level worked out from positions that were no longer open.

A pending order you placed by hand can now be taken into a chain from the Positions tab, the same way as an open position. It stays exactly as you placed it until you level the chain. From then on it carries the chain's stop and target and is cancelled with the chain, and it joins the chain's average once it fills.

After a hedge fills, its stop and target now follow the fill a few seconds later, so the loss at the stop is the amount you confirmed. The lots never change, and nothing is sent when the fill moved by less than 1% of the stop distance. You can turn this off under Settings, Execution.

Moving or closing a hedge's leg no longer fails when the terminal's Toolbox is showing History or another tab. The application switches to the Trade tab for the action and then back to the tab you had open.
The switch under the Positions tab's buttons is no longer cut off at the bottom of the panel, and turning it on or off no longer says "Not done".
In the calculator, "To lose" is now the full distance to the firm's floor. On an account in profit that is more than the drawdown allowance, because the floor does not rise with profit.

When a plan cannot be armed, the calculator now says which terminal to log into and offers to switch to a plan that can be armed right away. The plan picker shows which plans are logged in, and a new login is noticed within seconds instead of half a minute.

The funded plan card shows your share of the profit as a ring. Its profit bar marks where a payout covers everything the plan has cost and where you withdraw, payout dates appear as dates instead of "just now", and the fee refund from the first payout is counted. The card asks for a payout only once the firm will pay it.

A funded plan now says a payout is worth asking for when your share of it, together with the fee refund the first payout brings, gives back 120% of everything the plan has cost so far. You can change the 120% under Settings, Sizing. A withdrawal goal you typed yourself is left as it is.

From the second position of a challenge, the hedge ratio the calculator suggests is based on what the hedging on that account has actually come to, whether the prop side is behind or ahead. It used to fall back to the stage budget when the prop side was ahead. And when the suggested ratio is more than your broker account can carry to the target, the calculator says so and how much more the broker account would need.

Trading days are now counted the way the firm counts them: only days on which a position was opened, so a position held for several days counts once. A challenge that reaches its target before its trading days are done no longer asks you to request the next account. It says how many days are left and to trade them at the smallest volume, which the firm allows.

A hedge is no longer closed because its terminal was logged into a different account. Adding an account to a terminal while a hedge was open used to close the other leg within seconds, and tell you that you had closed it yourself. Nothing is closed now, firing is refused while a terminal is showing another account, and the hedge's row names the account to log back into. Separately, one hedge that cannot be read no longer stops the rest being watched: with two challenges running, a single terminal misbehaving used to leave the other hedge unguarded and say nothing about it.

A hedge whose terminal has been logged into another account now raises a window you cannot close, on whatever page you are on, naming the account to log back into, and it sounds an alarm when it appears. Log that account back in and the window goes by itself. If the account is not coming back, the window will close the leg on the terminal that still answers.

The hedge ratio the calculator suggests now counts every position on the challenge account, including the ones no broker trade ever answered. A trade you took on the prop side alone still moves the account towards its floor, so leaving it out asked the broker side to give back more than it had to: on one real account the suggestion falls from 12.93% to 8.87%. The figures beside it say which money each one is, and the hedge detail page no longer adds a prop dollar to a broker dollar.

Before a market closes, a window counts down and offers to close the hedges that are still open, or to leave them and stop it happening again until the next close. Doing nothing closes them at the time you set. That is the same setting that already refuses to arm near a close, because it is the same idea: near a close nothing new goes on and nothing open stays on. You will find it under Driving the terminals, and it reads the closing time from the desk expert on your chart.

A market that shuts early, for a public holiday or anything else, is now caught. Once your broker stops taking new positions in an instrument, any hedge open on it is closed there and then, instead of waiting for a published closing time that has already been and gone. The message says which of the two closed it, the countdown or the broker. This works on every terminal the product drives, including the ones with no desk on the chart.

The application no longer fills your disk with a record of changes for a shared journal you never turned on. On one machine that record had grown to 4.6 GB, which was almost the whole database. The next time the application starts it clears the record and gives the space back, saying so on the startup screen while it works. None of your own figures are touched, and if you do share a journal, nothing is thrown away that still has somewhere to go.

A hedge no longer closes the leg that is still open when the other one is taken. The two legs sit at the same price on two different feeds, so one of them is always taken a moment before the other, and closing the survivor at that moment was closing it feet from its own target. Two traders lost a challenge to it, thirty and a hundred and forty dollars short of passing. A leg with no target of its own is still closed at once, because nothing else would close it.

What you arm is what is sent. The lots and the levels you confirmed no longer change between arming and firing, and Arm opens a window showing the exact trade with Fire in it and no countdown. If the market has moved too far from a price you typed, firing is refused with the reason rather than sent at a different size. The setting for what stays fixed while the price moves has gone, because nothing moves any more.

What an account has left to lose is measured from where it stands now, not from the deepest it has ever been, so an account that has recovered is no longer told it has less room than it has. On a $25,000 account sitting $2,215 down against a floor $3,000 below its opening balance, that is $784.61 rather than $300.61. What was spent at its worst is still reported, and is still what a breach turns on.

From the second position of a challenge, the suggested hedge ratio is what your hedging has actually returned on that account, moved half a point in the direction the account last went. It used to divide the stage budget every time. The budget still sets the first position, and a challenge that has been reset starts from it again. Filling to the balance you bought the account at moves the ratio the other way, the calculator says when hedges nobody has answered are part of the figure, and the size of the step is a setting under Sizing.

Where your firm lists one instrument under two names, the calculator sizes and arms against the name your account has actually traded rather than whichever one the terminal listed first. Settings, under Catalogues, shows any account where there is a choice and lets you say which name to use.
A terminal that has closed with a hedge still open can be started again from Sources. It used to refuse, which left the hedge with nothing watching it and no way to close it.

The Overview shows what you have earned over time, day by day, week by week or month by month depending on how far back you look. The running total is drawn above what each period earned, and the card names the four parts the total is made of.

The calculator has a padlock in the stop, the target, the prop lots and the hedge ratio. A locked field stays where you put it: changing the risk no longer moves lots you have set, and moving the entry no longer drags a locked level with it. A locked field turns brass, so you can see at a glance what you have pinned, and which padlocks you close is remembered for next time. Those four fields no longer carry up and down arrows, the stop and the target are wider, and each of them holds its own unit inside the box.

Reading the price is much faster. Pressing NOW fills the entry in well under a second instead of about two, and the spinner beside it turns while it reads. Following the market is now live: the entry updates the moment the terminal reports that the price has moved, rather than on a timer, and the stop and the target keep their distances as it moves. It stops when you press the toggle again, close the calculator, or leave the page.

The magic number and the order comment can be set separately for each leg in Settings, and either can be left empty. The desk expert's Positions tab has a switch that takes every position you open on that instrument into the chain by itself. A position this application is managing can now sit in a chain and count towards its average, and the desk never moves its stop or its target.

An update finishes the job itself. The desk expert this version ships is put on your charts without you pressing anything, and the update window says which terminal it is working on. A terminal you have not set up from here is left exactly as it was, with a line saying so.

Every table has a height and scrolls inside it, so a long one no longer stretches the page past everything below it. Rows still load as you reach them, and scrolling deep into a list no longer sends you back to the top a few seconds later.

Some hedges showed twice the volume and twice the money they were worth, and said the deals and the balance disagreed about the account. The deals had been recorded a second time on 19 September, when the way an account is referred to changed. Installing this puts the record right and works the figures out again. Your data is copied before anything touches it, as it is on every update.

The product refuses to arm when the plan already carries a hedge, whether the product placed it or you opened it yourself in MetaTrader, and on any of the plan's accounts. The line beside the button says why it is grey.

Sizing a hedge counts what the broker account has already put behind the positions it is holding. Sizing one on a broker that is already carrying another plan's hedge no longer reports a margin level the broker would never agree with.
The target no longer reads wrong in points or in money for the first moment after the calculator opens.
Positions with no counterpart and an account's ledger fill as you scroll rather than putting you through numbered pages, and Positions with no counterpart can be narrowed to one account.
